passages.title: How to read a figure
passages.text:
Every figure in these notes is already labelled, and each side carries its own length printed beside it.  Those printed labels are the only numbers to work from.  Never measure a drawing with a ruler.  A figure is drawn to be clear, not to scale, so a side marked twelve may look shorter than a side marked five.

Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside of a shape.  Start at any corner, travel along every edge once, and finish at the corner you started from.  Add the labels together as you go.  The most common mistake is getting back to the start and carrying on, which counts one edge twice.

Two marks turn up again and again, and both are worth learning now.  A small square drawn inside a corner means that corner is a right angle, exactly ninety degrees.  Short ticks drawn across two sides mean those sides are equal to each other, which is how a figure tells you about a side it never labelled.

Perimeter measures the boundary.  Area measures the space shut inside that boundary.  They answer different questions, and multiplying two side lengths gives you area, never perimeter.

passages.title: Naming a shape
passages.text:
A triangle takes two names at once, and they answer different questions.  The first name describes its sides.  Scalene means no two sides match.  Isosceles means exactly two match.  Equilateral means all three match.  Ticks drawn across two sides are how a figure tells you they are equal without printing the same number twice.

The second name describes its corners.  Acute means every corner is smaller than a square corner.  Right means one corner is exactly square, and a figure marks that with a small square.  Obtuse means one corner opens wider than square.  A triangle can only ever have one corner that is right or obtuse, so those names are never shared.

Quadrilateral names work differently, because they nest inside one another.  A rectangle is any four-sided shape with four right angles and equal opposite sides.  A rhombus is any four-sided shape with four equal sides.  A square meets both of those, so a square is a rectangle and a rhombus at the same time.

That nesting runs in one direction only.  Every square is a rectangle, but most rectangles are certainly not squares.  When a question asks for the most exact name available, a wider name that happens to be true still counts as the wrong answer.

passages.title: Reading a decimal out loud
passages.text:
A decimal is read in three parts.  Say the whole number first, then say the word AND for the point itself, then read every digit after the point as a single whole number.  Finish by naming the place the LAST digit lands in.  So 3.24 is read three AND twenty-four hundredths, because the 4 sits in the hundredths place.

The place names run in order.  One digit after the point is tenths.  Two digits is hundredths.  Three digits is thousandths.  Counting the digits is therefore the whole trick, and it works in both directions.

Going backwards is the harder direction and the one worth practising.  Given the words, the place name at the end tells you exactly how many digits belong after the point.  Thousandths means three, so eight thousandths is written 0.008 rather than 0.8, and those two zeros are doing real work.

A zero straight after the point is never decoration.  It holds a place, and removing it shifts every digit behind it into a different place and changes the value of the number.

passages.title: Finding the rule
passages.text:
A growing pattern is a set of figures where each one is built from the one before it by adding the same amount.  The figures are numbered, and figure 1 is where the counting starts.  Three figures is enough to see what is happening, which is why three is what you are usually given.

Work out the growth first.  Count the dots in each figure, then find the difference between figure 1 and figure 2, and between figure 2 and figure 3.  Those two differences are equal in every pattern here, and that shared number is how much the pattern grows each step.

The rule multiplies the figure number by that growth.  If a pattern grows by 3 each step, the rule starts as 3 times n, where n stands for the figure number.  Then check it against figure 1.  If the rule gives fewer dots than figure 1 actually has, the difference is a fixed group.  It sits in every figure, and it gets added on the end.

A rule earns its keep on the figures nobody would draw.  Figure 100 takes one line of arithmetic with a rule and an entire evening without one.  That is the whole reason for writing the rule down instead of counting on.

passages.title: Reading a display
passages.text:
A display turns a pile of numbers into a picture, and reading one starts with a single bar.  Follow the top of the bar straight across to the scale up the side, and read the line it lands on.  Comparing bars, or adding them up, is built on getting that one reading right.

The same two questions come up again and again.  How many MORE is always one bar taken away from another, and never a sum.  The TOTAL is every bar added together, including the short ones that are easy to skip.

A bar graph and a histogram look alike, and they are not the same thing.  A bar graph sorts data into named groups, such as dog, cat and fish, and its bars are drawn with gaps.  Those names do not run into each other, so the bars do not either.  A histogram sorts numbers into intervals instead, such as 0 to 9 and 10 to 19.  Its bars touch, because one interval runs straight into the next along a number line.

That gap between the bars is information rather than decoration.  Sorting numbers into groups costs you something as well.  A histogram may show 13 students in the 20 to 29 interval, but it cannot tell you how long any one of them read for.

levels.name: Walk the Edge
levels.goal: Find the perimeter of a labelled figure, from a rectangle to an L-shape.

briefing.title: What perimeter is
lines: Perimeter is the distance all the way round the outside of a shape.  Picture walking the edge of a field and ending back where you started.
Every figure here is labelled, so you never measure the drawing.  Add the labels, going round once, and count every side exactly one time.
Watch for the trap.  Multiplying two sides gives you AREA, the space inside.  That is a different question, and it is the one this app used to ask.

levels.name: Name the Shape
levels.goal: Name a triangle by its sides and by its angles, and give a quadrilateral its most exact name.

briefing.title: Two names, not one
lines: A triangle gets TWO names, and they answer different questions.  One describes its sides.  Scalene means no two match, isosceles means exactly two match, equilateral means all three match.
The other describes its corners.  Acute means every corner is smaller than a square corner.  Right means one corner is exactly square.  Obtuse means one corner opens wider than square.

Quadrilaterals work differently.  Their names nest inside each other, so a square is also a rectangle and also a rhombus.  When a question asks for the most exact name, a wider name that is still true is the wrong answer.

levels.name: Say the Number
levels.goal: Read a decimal into words, and read the words back into a decimal.

briefing.title: Both directions
lines: Reading a decimal has a rule.  Say the whole number, say AND for the point, read the digits after it as one whole number, then name the place the last digit sits in.
So 3.24 is three AND twenty-four hundredths.  Two digits after the point means hundredths.  Count the digits and the place names itself.
The harder direction is going back.  Given the words, the place name tells you how many digits belong after the point.  Eight thousandths is 0.008, and those zeros are doing real work.

levels.name: Find the Rule
levels.goal: Read a growing pattern, write the rule behind it, and use the rule to reach figure 100.

briefing.title: Three figures, one rule
lines: A growing pattern adds the same number of dots every step.  You get figures 1, 2 and 3, and your job is to work out what is being added and where it starts.
Count the dots, then find the jump from figure 1 to figure 2, and from 2 to 3.  Those jumps are equal.  That number is what n gets multiplied by.
Then test your rule on figure 1.  If it comes up short, the difference is a fixed group sitting in every figure, and it is added on the end.
The point of a rule is figure 100.  Drawing it would take all evening.  The rule answers it in one line.

levels.name: Read the Chart
levels.goal: Read a bar graph and a histogram, compare their bars, and tell the two kinds apart.

briefing.title: Bars and what they mean
lines: Reading a display starts with one bar.  Follow its top straight across to the scale up the side and read the line it lands on.  Comparing and totalling come after that.
How many MORE is always a subtraction between two bars.  The TOTAL is every bar added up, including the short ones.

A bar graph and a histogram look alike.  A bar graph sorts named categories and leaves gaps between its bars.  A histogram groups numbers into intervals, and its bars touch, because one interval runs straight into the next.

levels.name: Review and Preview
levels.goal: Come back to every skill in the pack, each one asked a way it was not asked before.

briefing.title: Everything so far, asked backwards
lines: This level mixes all five earlier ones, and none of the questions are the ones you have already answered.
A perimeter arrives already worked out, and what is wanted is the square that matches it.  A pattern gives you the dot count and asks which figure it belongs to.
Decimals get lined up against each other, which is where the longest number turns out not to be the biggest.
The last kind is new:  not reading a display, but choosing which display could answer a question at all.

items.stem: One display groups its data into number intervals like 0 to 9 and 10 to 19, and its bars touch.  What is that display called?

distractorRationale.1: A bar graph sorts data into named categories such as dog or bus, and its bars are drawn with gaps between them because the categories do not join.
distractorRationale.2: A dot plot marks one dot per value along a number line.  It shows every single value, not counts inside intervals.
distractorRationale.3: A stem-and-leaf plot splits each number into a stem and a leaf, so the original values can still be read back.  A histogram cannot be read back that way.

items.explain: A histogram groups numbers into intervals and counts how many fall in each one, so its bars touch:  the intervals join with no gap between them.  That touching is the visible difference, and it is there because the horizontal axis is a number line rather than a list of names.

items.stem: Why are the bars of a histogram drawn touching, while the bars of a bar graph have gaps between them?
choices: Because a histogram usually holds more data.
Because a histogram's intervals join up along a number line, and a bar graph's categories do not.
Because histograms are always drawn taller.
Because a bar graph is allowed only four bars.

distractorRationale.0: The amount of data makes no difference.  A histogram of ten values still touches, and a bar graph of a thousand still has gaps.
distractorRationale.2: Height comes from the counts, not the type of display.  Either kind can be tall or short.
distractorRationale.3: A bar graph can have any number of categories.  The number of bars is not what separates the two.

items.explain: The gap is information.  A histogram's bottom axis is a number line, so 0 to 9 runs straight into 10 to 19 with nothing missing between them, and the bars touch to show it.  A bar graph's bottom axis is a list of separate names, and the gaps say those categories do not run into each other.

items.stem: You want to know how many students read for between 20 and 29 minutes.  Which display answers that?
choices: a histogram of how many minutes each student read
a bar graph of which pet each child keeps
a bar graph of how each student travels to school
a histogram of how tall each seedling is

distractorRationale.1: This sorts children by pet.  It never mentions minutes, so no bar on it can answer a question about reading time.
distractorRationale.2: This sorts students by how they travel.  It counts students, but not by how long they read.
distractorRationale.3: This is the right KIND of display and the wrong data.  Grouping into intervals only helps if the intervals are made of the thing you asked about.

items.explain: Two things have to match, and only one option gets both right.  The DATA has to be the thing you asked about, and the KIND has to fit it:  named groups go in a bar graph, numbers grouped into intervals go in a histogram.  That leaves a histogram of how many minutes each student read.
